publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Evolution to Synchronous Networks

articleTitle: Deployment strategy for transmission networks based on the synchronous digital hierarchy
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Evolution to Synchronous Networks
abstract: Transmission networks based on the synchronous digital hierarchy (SDH) offer a number of significant advantages over existing networks particularly in terms of the ability to manage the bandwidth. The paper reviews the nature of client networks and then examines two candidate deployment strategies which seek to optimise the support of client networks. The possible evolution of asynchronous transfer mode (ATM)-based client networks is also reviewed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The effect of evolution on synchronous equipment interfaces
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Evolution to Synchronous Networks
abstract: The new synchronous digital hierarchy (SDH) offers telecom operators the opportunity to build a managed flexible transport network. Such a network would offer bandwidth flexibility and capability of handling any type of service. However, the period of transition from today's network to a synchronous network based on SDH principles is critical to the successful deployment of SDH equipment. Improper specifications of interfaces or definition of functions could lead to a perpetuation of existing interface requirement even in an all synchronous network where some of the existing interfaces capabilities may be inappropriate. The paper examines today's network and the impact of evolution to the SDH network on equipment interface requirements and specifications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Synchronous networking of undersea cable systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Evolution to Synchronous Networks
abstract: TAT-9 (transatlantic optical system) will link USA, Canada, France, UK and Spain with the first synchronous undersea cable network using UBMs (undersea branching multiplexes) operating at 591.2 Mbit/s. The authors discuss the architecture and reasons why the particular method of data formatting was adopted. The advantage offered by undersea multiplexing is that security, fault tolerance and traffic flexibility can all be built into the network. The TAT-9 scheme produced a common optical interconnect data format between the major undersea cable system suppliers before the American SONET and CCITT synchronous digital hierarchy (SDH) standards were finalised. Future submarine networks will have to interface to SDH traffic so they discuss whether the TAT-9 standard should be maintained whilst making the system transparent to SDH data signals.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Network architecture for SDH transmission networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Evolution to Synchronous Networks
abstract: In order to develop the new generation of network management and control systems it is necessary to understand in more depth the underlying architectural features of what is now a very complex network situation. The network must be modelled from a number of different perspectives to reveal the underlying structures which are obscured by the high degree of functional integration supported by the synchronous digital hierarchy (SDH). A functional model is described which has been developed to describe the SDH network but is believed to be generally applicable to other network domains. This in turn leads to an information model which appears to suggest a solution to the essential network management paradox of reconciling logical integration with physical and logical diversity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Planning for a synchronous transmission bearer network
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Evolution to Synchronous Networks
abstract: Covers some aspects inherent in planning for evolution from an asynchronous to a synchronous transmission bearer network. Major influences affecting the present day asynchronous transmission network are examined, the shortcomings highlighted and the driving forces examined. Technical and operational benefits of synchronous networks are anticipated that will be enjoyed by network planners. A possible family of equipment based on the synchronous digital hierarchy (SDH) is described, in terms of functionality and networking abilities. Aspects of SDH network design and an outline of possible SDH network structure is given showing the application of the SDH equipment described. A possible evolutionary path from an existing asynchronous network to an SDH Network is also described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Evolution to Synchronous Networks
abstract: There are a range of techniques which can be employed to make a fault-tolerant network. Some are best used in isolated portions of a larger network whilst others can be employed effectively on a network-wide basis. The aim of a fault-tolerant network is a high level of circuit availability as perceived by the customer, but this of course can only be achieved at some cost to the operator. In simplest terms this extra cost is due to the increased hardware needed to provide standby circuits through the network. However, two other important cost factors must be allowed for, namely the cost of the control mechanisms (for example software) used to ensure that failed circuits are restored and the cost of extra maintenance staff. A comparison is included of the available protection techniques listed in order of increasing complexity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ISDN synchronization-the view from a clock manufacturer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Evolution to Synchronous Networks
abstract: Illustrates with examples alternative solutions to present day synchronization requirements of some public and private networks. Digital networks as they stand today pose a particular set of timing problems. In general these are now well defined and well met with current technology. As one moves towards the synchronous digital hierarchy and SONET a new set of rules are met, some as yet still evolving and not well defined or understood. Yet, by the very nature of the philosophy of SDH it will be essential to operate a superlative clock system. In addition, the ability to distribute, disseminate and regenerate without losing the intrinsic accuracy of this clock throughout the network will be of paramount importance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
